lessons.title: Components of a Good Potting Mix
lessons.body: A good potting mix is not just garden soil. It must hold water, drain well, and allow air to reach roots. The ideal mix has three parts: organic matter (compost or well-rotted manure), aeration material (rice hulls, sawdust, or coarse sand), and a moisture-holding base (topsoil or coconut coir). In Africa, you can use locally available materials. For example, mix 2 parts sieved compost, 1 part river sand, and 1 part rice hulls. If rice hulls are not available, use groundnut shells crushed small. Avoid using fresh manureâit burns seedlings. Also avoid heavy clay soil; it becomes hard and cracks. A simple test: squeeze a handful of moist mix. It should form a ball that breaks apart when you poke it. If it stays sticky, add more sand or hulls. If it crumbles, add more compost. You can also add a little wood ash for potassium, but no more than a handful per wheelbarrow of mix. Remember, seedlings are delicate. Their roots need fine particles, so sift your compost through a wire mesh (5 mm holes) before mixing. Never use soil from under a tree where seedlings of the same family have grownâit may carry diseases. For a standard nursery bed, a mix of 3 parts compost, 2 parts sand, and 1 part topsoil works well for most vegetables like tomatoes, onions, and cabbage. For trees like mango or avocado, use more sand for drainage. Always test your mix with a few seeds before filling all your trays. A good mix smells earthy, not sour. If it smells bad, it is too wet or not decomposed. Keep your mix slightly moist, not soaking. This simple recipe can save you money and give you strong, healthy seedlings.

lessons.title: Sterilizing Soil and Media
lessons.body: Sterilizing your potting mix kills weed seeds, insect eggs, and disease-causing germs. This is critical because seedlings are easily killed by damping-off, a fungal disease that makes stems rot at the soil line. You can sterilize small amounts of mix using a pot of boiling water. Put the mix in a bucket, pour boiling water until it is soaked, cover with a lid, and let it cool. This kills most pathogens. For larger amounts, use solarization: spread the mix in a thin layer (10 cm deep) on black plastic, cover with clear plastic, and leave in full sun for 2-3 days. The heat builds up and kills pests. Another method is baking: put moist mix in a metal tray, cover with foil, and bake at 180Â°C for 30 minutes. It will smell, so do it outdoors. After sterilizing, let the mix cool completely before planting. Do not sterilize with chemicals like formalin unless you have trainingâit is dangerous. Also, sterilizing kills good microbes, so after cooling, mix in a handful of fresh compost to reintroduce beneficial organisms. For small-scale farmers, solarization is cheapest and safest. In hot African climates, you can solarize in one day. If you have no plastic, you can pour boiling water over the mix in a wheelbarrow, turn it, and cover with a tarpaulin. Always wear gloves and a mask when handling hot mix. Sterilized mix should be used within a week, as it can be re-contaminated. Store it in clean sacks or bins. Remember, prevention is better than cure: clean your tools, trays, and hands before working with sterilized mix. This step alone can increase your seedling survival rate from 50% to over 90%.

lessons.title: Mixing Your Own Seedling Mix
lessons.body: Mixing your own seedling mix saves money and gives you control. Start with a clean, flat surface like a concrete floor or a large tarp. You will need: a wheelbarrow, a shovel, a watering can, and a sieve (wire mesh with 5-10 mm holes). Gather your ingredients: compost (well-rotted, at least 6 months old), coarse sand, and rice hulls or sawdust. A basic recipe: 3 buckets of compost, 2 buckets of sand, and 1 bucket of rice hulls. If your compost is heavy clay, add extra sand. If it is sandy, add extra compost. Sift all ingredients to remove stones and lumps. Then mix thoroughly by turning the pile three times. While turning, sprinkle water to keep the mix moist but not wet. The final mix should be crumbly. Test by squeezing: it should hold together lightly and break with a touch. Now, add nutrients. For every wheelbarrow of mix, add 1 cup of wood ash (for potassium) and 1 cup of crushed eggshells (for calcium). If you have bone meal, add 2 cups. Mix again. Do not add chemical fertilizers at this stageâthey can burn seedlings. Fill your trays or nursery beds with the mix, press gently, and water before sowing. Let the mix settle for a day before planting. This allows moisture to distribute evenly. For different crops, adjust: leafy vegetables like more compost; root crops like more sand. Always label your mix with the date and ingredients. Use within one month. If you see mold, it is too wetâadd more hulls. This mix costs a fraction of store-bought and uses local materials. Many farmers in Kenya and Nigeria use this method successfully.

lessons.title: Using Compost and Organic Matter
lessons.body: Compost is the heart of any seedling mix. It provides nutrients, holds water, and improves soil structure. But not all compost is equal. You need fully decomposed compostâdark, crumbly, and smelling like forest soil. If it still looks like kitchen scraps or smells sour, it is not ready. To make good compost, layer green materials (kitchen waste, grass clippings) with brown materials (dry leaves, straw, cardboard) in a pile. Keep it as moist as a squeezed sponge. Turn it every two weeks. In 2-3 months, it will be ready. You can also use well-rotted manure from cows, goats, or chickens. But manure must be aged for at least 6 months to kill weed seeds and pathogens. Never use fresh manure. For seedlings, compost should be sifted through a 5 mm sieve to remove large pieces. A good ratio in your mix is 30-50% compost by volume. More than that can make the mix too heavy and hold too much water. You can also use worm castings (vermicompost) â they are rich and fine, perfect for seedlings. If you have no compost, you can use leaf mold: collect fallen leaves, pile them, keep moist, and wait 6-12 months. It is lower in nutrients but good for aeration. Another option is coconut coir, but it is expensive. In Africa, many farmers use rice hulls, groundnut shells, or coffee husks as organic matter. These are not compost but add aeration. Remember, organic matter breaks down over time, so your mix will shrink. That is normal. Always mix compost with other ingredients; pure compost can crust and repel water. Test your compost by planting a few bean seeds in it. If they grow well, it is safe. If they die, your compost may be too salty or immature. Use it as mulch instead.

lessons.title: pH and Nutrient Requirements for Seedlings
lessons.body: pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is. It ranges from 0 to 14. Most seedlings grow best between pH 6.0 and 7.0 (slightly acidic to neutral). If pH is too low (acidic), nutrients like phosphorus get locked up. If too high (alkaline), iron and zinc become unavailable. In Africa, many soils are acidic, especially in high-rainfall areas. You can test pH with a simple kit from an agro-vet shop. It costs a few dollars. Or use red cabbage indicator: boil red cabbage, collect the purple water, add a spoonful of soil, and watch the color. Pink means acidic, blue means alkaline. For seedlings, you need to adjust pH before planting. If too acidic (pH below 5.5), add agricultural lime (calcium carbonate). A common rate is 1 cup per square meter of nursery bed, mixed into the top 15 cm. If too alkaline (pH above 7.5), add elemental sulfur or gypsum. But be carefulâchanges take weeks. For small seedling trays, use a mix that is already balanced. Compost usually has a pH near neutral. Avoid adding wood ash in large amountsâit raises pH quickly. Nutrients: seedlings need nitrogen (N) for leaves, phosphorus (P) for roots, and potassium (K) for stems. A good compost provides these slowly. But if your seedlings look yellow or stunted, they may need a boost. Use a weak liquid fertilizer: mix 1 tablespoon of fish emulsion or worm tea in 1 liter of water, and apply every 2 weeks. Do not over-fertilizeâit burns roots. For organic options, use manure tea: soak a sack of aged manure in a barrel of water for 3 days, then dilute 1:10 with water. Always water seedlings before applying fertilizer to prevent burn. Test your pH once a year, and adjust your mix accordingly.

lessons.title: Testing and Adjusting Soil pH
lessons.body: Testing pH is simple and cheap. You can buy a pH test kit from any farm supply store. It comes with a test tube, a color chart, and a powder. Mix a spoonful of soil with distilled water (or rain water), add the powder, and compare the color. Or use a digital pH meterâthey cost about $20 and are more accurate. For a DIY test, use vinegar and baking soda. Put a spoonful of soil in a cup. Add a few drops of vinegar. If it fizzes, your soil is alkaline (pH above 7). If no fizz, take another sample, add water to make mud, then add baking soda. If it fizzes, your soil is acidic (pH below 6). This gives you a rough idea. For seedlings, you want pH 6.0-7.0. If your test shows pH 5.0, you need to raise it. Add lime: for a nursery bed of 1 m x 1 m, mix in 2 cups of agricultural lime. Water well. Wait 2 weeks before planting. If pH is 8.0, lower it with elemental sulfur: 1 cup per square meter. Or add plenty of compost, which naturally buffers pH. Another option is to use a soilless mix: coconut coir and compost have near-neutral pH. If you are using soil from your farm, test it first. Adjusting pH takes time, so do it before sowing. For small trays, you can make a mix with 50% compost, 30% sand, and 20% topsoilâthis usually gives pH around 6.5. If you cannot test, plant a few indicator crops: potatoes and strawberries like acidic soil; beans and cabbage like neutral. If they grow poorly, test and adjust. Always keep records of your pH and what you added, so you learn for next season. Remember, extreme pH (below 4 or above 9) is rare, but if you have it, use raised beds with imported mix. Regular composting and mulching help maintain good pH over time.

quiz.q: What are the three main components of a good potting mix?
options: B) Organic matter, aeration material, and moisture-holding base
quiz.explanation: A good potting mix needs organic matter for nutrients, aeration material for air, and a base to hold moisture.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good aeration material for seedling mix?
quiz.explanation: Rice hulls are lightweight and create air spaces in the mix.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to check if your potting mix has the right moisture?
options: A) Squeeze a handful; it should form a ball that breaks when poked
B) Pour water until it pools on top
D) Add more sand until it crumbles
quiz.explanation: A ball that breaks apart indicates good moisture and texture.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using fresh manure in seedling mix?
quiz.explanation: Fresh manure is high in salts and ammonia, which can burn delicate seedling roots.

quiz.q: What size sieve is recommended for sifting compost for seedlings?
quiz.explanation: A 5 mm mesh removes large lumps while keeping fine particles.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of sterilizing soil and media?
options: B) To kill weed seeds, pests, and diseases
quiz.explanation: Sterilization eliminates harmful organisms that can kill seedlings.

quiz.q: Which method is cheapest and safest for small-scale farmers to sterilize mix?
quiz.explanation: Solarization uses the sun's heat and is low-cost and safe.

quiz.q: After sterilizing, why should you add a handful of fresh compost?
quiz.explanation: Sterilization kills good microbes too, so adding compost restores them.

quiz.q: How long should you solarize a thin layer of mix in full sun?
quiz.explanation: Two to three days of full sun is enough to kill most pathogens.

quiz.q: What should you do if your sterilized mix smells bad after cooling?
quiz.explanation: A bad smell indicates re-contamination or incomplete sterilization; it is unsafe.

quiz.q: What is a basic recipe for a seedling mix by volume?
options: A) 1 part compost, 1 part sand, 1 part topsoil
B) 3 parts compost, 2 parts sand, 1 part rice hulls
quiz.explanation: This ratio provides good balance of nutrients, drainage, and aeration.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid adding chemical fertilizers directly to seedling mix?
options: D) They make the mix too light
quiz.explanation: Chemical fertilizers are concentrated and can damage tender roots.

quiz.q: How many times should you turn the pile when mixing your own seedling mix?
quiz.explanation: Turning three times ensures thorough mixing of ingredients.

quiz.q: What can you add to your mix for potassium?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is a good source of potassium, but use sparingly.

quiz.q: How long should you let your mixed seedling mix settle before planting?
quiz.explanation: One day allows moisture to distribute evenly.

quiz.q: What is the ideal stage of compost for seedling mix?
options: C) Fully decomposed, dark and crumbly
quiz.explanation: Fully decomposed compost is safe and rich in nutrients.

quiz.q: How long should manure be aged before using in seedling mix?
quiz.explanation: Aging for 6 months kills weed seeds and pathogens.

quiz.q: What percentage of compost by volume is recommended in a seedling mix?
quiz.explanation: 30-50% compost provides nutrients without making the mix too heavy.

quiz.q: What is vermicompost?
quiz.explanation: Vermicompost is worm castings, rich and fine for seedlings.

quiz.q: Why should you not use pure compost as a seedling mix?
options: B) It can crust and repel water
quiz.explanation: Pure compost can become hydrophobic and compact, harming roots.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for most seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Most seedlings grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil.

quiz.q: What does a pH of 5.5 indicate?
quiz.explanation: pH below 7 is acidic.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is important for root development in seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus supports root growth.

quiz.q: What is a sign that seedlings need a nutrient boost?
quiz.explanation: Yellowing and stunting often indicate nutrient deficiency.

quiz.q: How should you apply liquid fertilizer to seedlings?
options: B) Dilute with water and apply every 2 weeks
C) Spray on leaves in full sun
quiz.explanation: Diluted fertilizer is gentle and should be applied regularly but not too often.

quiz.q: What is a simple DIY test for soil pH using vinegar?
options: A) If it fizzes, soil is acidic
B) If it fizzes, soil is alkaline
C) If it turns blue, soil is neutral
D) If it smells, soil is fertile
quiz.explanation: Vinegar reacts with alkaline soil (calcium carbonate) to produce fizz.

quiz.q: What should you add to raise pH if it is too low?
options: D) Wood ash in large amounts
quiz.explanation: Lime is calcium carbonate and raises pH.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after adding lime before planting?
quiz.explanation: Lime needs time to react and change pH.

quiz.q: What is a soilless mix that usually has near-neutral pH?
quiz.explanation: Coir and compost are balanced and do not have extreme pH.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of pH adjustments?
options: A) To show off to neighbors
B) To learn and improve next season
quiz.explanation: Records help you understand what works and make better decisions.
